name: Guru Granth Sahib
info: The Guru Granth Sahib is the central scripture of Sikhism, which Sikhs regard as their final and eternal Guru. Guru Arjan compiled its first rendition, the Adi Granth, in 1604, and Guru Gobind Singh completed the canon in the early 1700s.

facts.made: Compiled by the fifth guru, Guru Arjan, with Bhai Gurdas as scribe; composed predominantly by six Sikh gurus, with hymns of Hindu Bhakti sants and the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid
facts.form: 1,430 angs (pages) and 5,894 shabads, set in rāgas and written in the Gurmukhi script in many languages, among them Punjabi, Sanskrit, Braj Bhasha, Persian and Arabic
facts.where: Installed in Sikh gurdwaras; early manuscripts include Guru Nanak Dev University Manuscript 1245 and a 1707 Damdama bir at the Toshakhana in Nanded; official copies are printed in Amritsar
facts.known: regarded by Sikhs as the living Guru; hymns arranged by rāga and set to music; the Mul Mantar and Japji Sahib of Guru Nanak; verses of Kabir and Sheikh Farid; the daily prakash and sukhasan rituals; the Gurmukhi script

t: Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as the final, sovereign and eternal Guru, following the ten human gurus, and treat it with the honours due to a living person.
Guru Arjan compiled its first rendition in 1604, and Guru Gobind Singh added the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur to produce the final edition.
Its hymns are arranged mainly by the rāga in which they are sung, and they include verses by Hindu Bhakti sants and a Muslim Sufi saint as well as by the gurus.
dyk: Copies of the Guru Granth Sahib that are no longer fit to be read from are cremated, in a ceremony similar to the one for a deceased person, called Agan Bheta.
ev: The oldest surviving manuscript of the Adi Granth, Guru Nanak Dev University Manuscript 1245, is dated to about this time
Guru Arjan completes the Adi Granth, which is installed in the Golden Temple in Amritsar with Baba Buddha as the first granthi
At Damdama Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh and Bhai Mani Singh add the compositions of Guru Tegh Bahadur to create the final edition
Guru Gobind Singh affirms the scripture as his successor shortly before his death
The first printed copy of the Guru Granth Sahib is made
Ernest Trumpp publishes the first philological study and a major but incomplete English translation
Max Arthur Macauliffe's six volume translation appears from Oxford University Press
Gopal Singh publishes the first complete English translation

sections.origins:
The Guru Granth Sahib is the central holy scripture of Sikhism. Sikhs regard it as the final, sovereign and eternal Guru, following the lineage of the ten human gurus of the religion. Its first rendition, the Adi Granth, was compiled by the fifth guru, Guru Arjan (1564–1606).

Its roots lie in the Kartarpur chapter of Guru Nanak's life, when his compositions were seen as a source of wisdom and gathered in a book known as a pothi. Guru Nanak's hymns were sung by his followers in rāga, a musical setting. His successor, Guru Angad, opened centres and distributed the hymns, and the community sang them while his agents collected donations. The third and fourth gurus continued the practice. The collection passed to Guru Angad, and he and the later gurus enlarged the Sikh scriptural corpus with their own works and those of others, in line with Sikh theology.

Guru Arjan found that Prithi Chand, his eldest brother and a rival claimant to the guruship, held a copy of an earlier pothi and was circulating hymns of the earlier gurus together with his own. Guru Arjan considered these spurious and wanted an authentic anthology of approved hymns.
sections.content:
The text consists of 1,430 angs (pages, a word meaning "limbs" in Sikh tradition) and 5,894 shabads (line compositions), poetically rendered and set to a rhythmic north Indian classical form of music. The bulk is divided into 31 main rāgas, each subdivided by length and author, and the hymns are arranged primarily by the rāgas in which they are read. The whole is written in the Gurmukhi script, in many languages including Punjabi, Lahnda, Sanskrit, Braj Bhasha, Awadhi, Sindhi, Marathi, Bengali, Persian and Arabic. Copies in these languages often carry the generic title Sant Bhasha.

It has three parts. An introductory section holds the Mul Mantar, Japji Sahib, So Dhar (Rehras) and Sohila, composed by Guru Nanak. The main body gives the compositions of the gurus, followed in each rāga by those of the bhagats. A closing section contains Sanskrit shaloks, the Gatha, Phunhe and Chaubole, the shaloks of Kabir and Farid, savaiye, the Mundawani and the Ragmala, a list of the rāgas. Rāga sections may also include recurring forms such as vars (ballad type poems), chhands, ashtapadiyan, pehre, Bara Maha (poems on the twelve months) and thithi.

The text sets out a vision of a society based on divine freedom, mercy, love and justice without oppression of any kind. It acknowledges and respects the scriptures of Hinduism and Islam but does not imply a moral reconciliation with either.
sections.making:
Guru Arjan began compiling an officially approved version of the scripture. He sent associates across the Indian subcontinent to collect circulating hymns of the gurus, and he persuaded Mohan, the son of Guru Amar Das, to give him the collection of the writings of the first three gurus. As the collections came in, Guru Arjan selected and edited hymns for the Adi Granth, with Bhai Gurdas as his scribe. The work yielded several drafts and manuscripts, some of which survive. The compilation was completed on 29 August 1604.

The Guru Granth Sahib was composed predominantly by six gurus: Guru Nanak, Guru Angad, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur. It also holds the teachings of Hindu Bhakti sants such as Ramananda, Kabir and Namdev, and of one Muslim Sufi saint, Sheikh Farid, along with verses by bards (Bhatts). In Sikh tradition Guru Hargobind is credited with adding the rāga tunes for nine of the 22 vars.

In 1704 at Damdama Sahib, during a year's respite from heavy fighting with the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, Guru Gobind Singh and Bhai Mani Singh added the compositions of Guru Tegh Bahadur to the Adi Granth to create the final edition, the Damdama bir. Guru Gobind Singh's own compositions were not included; they were set into the Dasam Granth.
sections.reception:
The scripture was revered even before it became guru. When it was first installed in the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar in 1604, on a cot under a canopy with a fly-whisk attendant, Guru Arjan bowed to it and sat at a lower level. Baba Buddha was its first granthi, or reader. In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh conferred the title "Guru of the Sikhs" upon the Adi Granth, an event recorded in a Bhatt Vahi (a bard's scroll) by an eyewitness, Narbud Singh. Sikhs since then have accepted it as their eternal living guru and as the embodiment of the ten gurus. Groups that tried to continue the guruship in human form were sidelined by the main faction, led by Mata Sundari and Bhai Mani Singh.

Its words may not be changed. This tradition is traced to Guru Har Rai, who barred his son Ram Rai from his presence after Ram Rai, to please Aurangzeb, altered a verse of Asa ki Var by replacing "Musalman" with "Beiman".

Colonial scholars translated it. Ernest Trumpp published a major but incomplete English translation in 1877; his remark that Sikhism was "a waning religion" offended many Sikhs, though Mark Juergensmeyer calls his scholarship still valuable. Max Arthur Macauliffe's six volumes (Oxford, 1909) were well received by Sikhs, though later scholars have called his handling of Sikh traditions "uncritical".
sections.survival:
The oldest surviving manuscript of the Adi Granth is Guru Nanak Dev University Manuscript 1245, dated to c. 1599. Other early editions include the Bahoval pothi (c. 1600), the Vanjara pothi (c. 1601) and the Bhai Rupa pothi (c. 1603). The Guru Harsahai pothi, kept by the Sodhis, is believed to be the one that existed before Guru Arjan's compilation. It was stolen in 1970 during a transfer, though photographs of some pages survive. The Sodhis claim it is the oldest and partly written by Guru Nanak, but that claim first appears in texts attributed to the 17th century Hariji, and the photographs make it unlikely that Guru Nanak wrote or kept a pothi.

When Guru Gobind Singh and his followers left Anandpur Sahib in 1704, manuscripts of the Ād Granth were left behind, and many were looted by the Pahari Rajas. Some came back into Sikh hands through purchases by later Sikh ruled polities such as the Sikh Empire and Patiala. A 1707 copy of the Damdama bir is preserved at the Toshakhana in Nanded.

Only handwritten copies were made until the late 19th century. Early printed editions appeared at Lahore, Gujranwala, Amritsar and Lucknow. Since the early 20th century it has been printed in a standard edition of 1,430 angs. Copies unfit for reading are cremated.
sections.legacy:
The scripture is the focal point of every gurdwara, seated on a raised platform called a takht while the congregation sits on the floor. Sikhs cover their heads and remove their shoes in its presence, and it is carried on the head, under a canopy, with a chaur (fan whisk) waved over it. A granthi cares for it and recites from it. In major gurdwaras such as the Golden Temple it is treated as a living person: at dawn the prakash ritual brings it from its bedroom in a palanquin and a page is opened at random, the first complete verse on the left page being the mukhwak of the day; at night the sukhasan ritual puts it to rest.

Official copies are produced in Amritsar by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), which the Akal Takht names as the only authorised publisher. On 9 May 1998 a hukamnama banned private publishing, and in 2007 the state of Punjab made it illegal for private firms to copy the scripture. In September 2023 the SGPC announced printing at Tracy, California, for Sikhs in North America.

Three stanzas read from it were used in a United Nations video released on 30 March 2021. Pearl S. Buck, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938, wrote that its scriptures "speak to persons of any religion or of none".

summary: The Guru Granth Sahib is the central scripture of Sikhism, which Sikhs regard as their eternal Guru. Guru Arjan compiled it in 1604 as the Adi Granth, and Guru Gobind Singh added the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur. It runs to 1,430 pages of hymns set in rāgas.
notes: start 1604 is the completion of the Adi Granth; the article gives no year for Guru Nanak's earliest compositions, and says the major expansions were around 1570, 1604, 1675 and the 1690s.

Contradictions in the article: the lead says fourteen Hindu Bhakti sants and one Muslim Sufi saint (Sheikh Farid); the Contributors section says thirteen Hindu and two Muslim. The text avoids the counts. It also says 31 main rāgas, but later lists sixty rāgas. The text gives 31 only.

The article gives the date of the final edition two ways: Guru Gobind Singh added Tegh Bahadur's hymns in 1704 at Damdama Sahib, and he affirmed the text as his successor on 6 October 1708. Both kept. The Damdama bir copy is 1707.

The article gives Pearl S. Buck's longer statement, which compares this scripture with other religions' scriptures; left out as a ranking. Only her line about speaking to people of any religion or none is quoted.

Left out: the Akali Nihang view of the Dasam and Sarbloh Granths as extensions, the weapons before the scripture, the five scholarly views of the manuscript tradition (thin on names, partly one sided), Trumpp's omission of 'one' in Ik Oankar, Sindhi translation, other English translations.
Article is thin on references: the Further reading lists only Trumpp 1877 and Macauliffe 1909 in digitised form; the editor may use those.
The 'Guru of the Sikhs' conferral in 1708 and the Narbud Singh Bhatt Vahi account are stated by the article as fact; the text follows that.
